# Linear algebra {#sec-linear-algebra}

Linear algebra is the study of vector spaces, the sets in which one can add and rescale, and of the maps between
them that respect those two operations. This chapter collects the part of it that geometry and field theory use on
every page, in four sections. Vector spaces defines spans, linear independence, bases and dimension, with
$\mathbb{R}^n$, spaces of matrices and spaces of functions as running examples. Linear maps and dual spaces treats
linear maps and their matrices, kernels and images, and the linear functionals that make up the dual space, with
the dual basis as the bridge between coordinates and functionals. Bilinear forms introduces the rule that assigns a
number to two vectors, with the Euclidean dot product and the Minkowski form of special relativity as the two
cases that matter most, and defines symmetry, non-degeneracy and signature. Multilinear maps and tensor products
generalises to maps of several arguments and to tensors of mixed type, their components and their contractions.
Each definition is followed by three examples of increasing complexity and three exercises of increasing
difficulty with hidden solutions, and each part closes with propositions that collect its key computations. The
reader who knows this material can skim the definitions and try the exercises; the exact conventions for indices and
the summation convention are fixed in @sec-conventions.

## Vector spaces {#sec-vector-spaces}

A vector space is a set in which vectors can be added and rescaled. The six notions of this section, vector
spaces, linear combinations, spans, linear independence, bases and dimension, are the vocabulary in which every
later definition is phrased; the two propositions at its end record two dimension counts and the coordinates of one
vector in a skewed basis.

### Vector spaces

Everything in this chapter rests on two operations, adding two vectors and stretching one by a number, together with
the rules those operations obey. The definition below lists the rules once and for all; the picture to keep is that of
arrows in the plane, added tip to tail and rescaled along their own line. It also names the subsets that inherit the
structure, the subspaces, which is where most of the work will happen.

:::: {.statement-box}
::: {#def-vector-space}
#### Vector space

A **real vector space** is a set $V$ with an addition $v + w$ and a multiplication $\lambda v$ by real numbers
(**scalars**) that obey the usual rules: addition is commutative and associative with a zero vector $0$ and
negatives, and $\lambda(v + w) = \lambda v + \lambda w$, $(\lambda + \mu) v = \lambda v + \mu v$, $(\lambda\mu) v =
\lambda(\mu v)$, $1 v = v$. Replacing $\mathbb{R}$ by $\mathbb{C}$ gives a **complex vector space**. A subset closed
under both operations is a **subspace**.
:::

The first instance is the one every reader already knows: columns of $n$ real numbers, added and rescaled entry by
entry. It also shows the subspace test at work in both directions, since a plane through the origin passes it while
the unit sphere does not.

::: {#exm-vs-rn}
#### $\mathbb{R}^n$

$\mathbb{R}^n$, the set of columns $(x^1, \dots, x^n)$, with entrywise addition and scaling, is a vector space;
the plane $\{x^3 = 0\}$ is a subspace of $\mathbb{R}^3$, while the sphere $S^2$ is not (the sum of two unit vectors
is not a unit vector).
:::

Vectors need not be columns. Square matrices add and rescale entrywise just as well, and applying the subspace test to
antisymmetric matrices on the one hand and to rotation matrices on the other separates a Lie algebra, which is a
vector space, from a Lie group, which is not.

::: {#exm-vs-matrices}
#### Matrices

The $n \times n$ real matrices form a vector space of dimension $n^2$ under entrywise operations; the
antisymmetric matrices $A^{\mathsf{T}} = -A$ form a subspace, the Lie algebra $\mathfrak{so}(n)$ of
@sec-lie-algebras. The rotation matrices $SO(n)$ do not: the sum of two rotations is not a rotation.
:::

`la-antisym-add-smul-test.sage` (kernel-checked instances): A + c B is antisymmetric for antisymmetric A, B, at n = 0, 2, 3 with explicit matrices, entry by entry.

`la-infeasible.sage`: Sage refutes the contradictory numeric or polynomial facts left by the hypothesis (a Nullstellensatz or Positivstellensatz certificate from a Gröbner lift or an exact LP), checked by `linear_combination`.
:::

The third instance has no finite list of coordinates at all. Functions on a set are added pointwise, so they form a
vector space that is usually infinite-dimensional, and the scalar fields of physics live in such a space; the
polynomials of bounded degree sit inside it as a finite-dimensional subspace.

::: {#exm-vs-functions}
#### Functions and fields

The real functions on a set $X$, with $(f + g)(x) = f(x) + g(x)$ and $(\lambda f)(x) = \lambda f(x)$, form a vector
space, infinite-dimensional when $X$ is infinite; the polynomials of degree at most $2$ form a three-dimensional
subspace. A scalar field on spacetime (@sec-scalar-fields) is an element of such a function space.
:::

:::: {.callout-note .exercises-fold collapse="true" title="Exercises"}
The subspace test, closure under addition and under rescaling, is best learned on sets that fail it for different
reasons. Three subsets of $\mathbb{R}^3$ follow, and the reader should identify a different culprit in each case: a
missing zero vector, or a sum that escapes the set.

::: {#exr-vs-subspace-check}
#### Which subsets are subspaces?

Decide whether the plane $x + y + z = 0$, the plane $x + y + z = 1$ and the union of the two coordinate axes are
subspaces of $\mathbb{R}^3$.
:::

::: {.callout-note .solution collapse="true" title="Solution"}
The plane $x + y + z = 0$ is a subspace: sums and multiples of solutions are solutions, and $0$ lies in it. The
plane $x + y + z = 1$ is not: it does not contain $0$, and the sum of two of its points has coordinate sum $2$. The
union of the axes is closed under scaling but not under addition: $(1, 0, 0) + (0, 1, 0) = (1, 1, 0)$ lies on
neither axis.
:::

::: {.callout-tip .verification collapse="true" title="Verification"}

The same test can be run in Sage, which becomes useful as soon as the sets are too large to inspect by hand. This time

::: {#exr-vs-symmetric-matrices}
#### Symmetric matrices and rotations

Show with Sage that the symmetric $3 \times 3$ matrices form a subspace of the $3 \times 3$ matrices, find its
dimension, and check that the sum of two rotation matrices is not a rotation.
:::

::: {.callout-note .solution collapse="true" title="Solution"}
$(A + B)^{\mathsf{T}} = A^{\mathsf{T}} + B^{\mathsf{T}} = A + B$ and $(\lambda A)^{\mathsf{T}} = \lambda A$, so
sums and multiples of symmetric matrices are symmetric; the matrices $E_{ii}$ and $E_{ij} + E_{ji}$ ($i < j$) span
the subspace, which has dimension $3 + 3 = 6$. Two rotations by $90^\circ$ about different axes add to a matrix
$R$ with $R^{\mathsf{T}} R \neq 1$:

{{< sage exr-vs-symmetric-matrices >}}
:::

Function spaces are checked in the same way, with pointwise operations in place of entrywise ones. The point of the
last exercise in this group is the difference between a bound on the degree, which gives a subspace, and an exact
degree, which does not; the same distinction appears whenever an expansion is truncated.

::: {#exr-vs-polynomials-axioms}
#### Polynomials of bounded degree

Show that the polynomials of degree at most $2$ form a subspace of the functions on $\mathbb{R}$, and that the
polynomials of degree exactly $2$ do not.
:::

::: {.callout-note .solution collapse="true" title="Solution"}
$(a + bx + cx^2) + (a' + b'x + c'x^2) = (a + a') + (b + b')x + (c + c')x^2$ and $\lambda(a + bx + cx^2) = \lambda a +
\lambda b x + \lambda c x^2$ have degree at most $2$, and the zero polynomial is included. The polynomials of
degree exactly $2$ miss the zero polynomial, and $x^2 + (-x^2 + x) = x$ has degree $1$: the set is closed under
neither operation.
:::

::: {.callout-tip .verification collapse="true" title="Verification"}

### Linear combinations

With addition and rescaling available, the simplest object one can build from a finite family of vectors is a weighted
sum of them. The definition that follows names this operation and fixes the index convention, upper indices on
coefficients and lower indices on vectors, on which every later formula relies.

:::: {.statement-box}
::: {#def-linear-combination}
#### Linear combination

A **linear combination** of vectors $v_1, \dots, v_k$ is a vector $\lambda^1 v_1 + \dots + \lambda^k v_k$ with real
coefficients $\lambda^i$. Repeated upper and lower indices are summed, $\lambda^i v_i$ (the summation convention of
@sec-conventions).
:::

:::: {.callout-note .examples-fold collapse="true" title="Examples"}
In coordinates a weighted sum is a sum of rescaled columns, and the standard basis vectors show that every column is
such a sum. The first example records one explicit combination of three-component columns; the same three vectors
return throughout the chapter as a running case.

::: {#exm-combination-r3}
#### In $\mathbb{R}^3$

$(1, 3, 1) = 1\cdot(1, 2, 0) + 1\cdot(0, 1, 1)$ is a linear combination of $(1, 2, 0)$ and $(0, 1, 1)$; every vector
$(x, y, z)$ is the combination $x e_1 + y e_2 + z e_3$ of the standard basis vectors.
:::

The same operation applied to the three generators of rotations produces every antisymmetric $3 \times 3$ matrix. This
is the first appearance of the pattern "general element equals weighted sum of generators" that the notion of span
will make precise in the next section.

::: {#exm-combination-matrices}
#### Antisymmetric matrices

$a L_1 + b L_2 + c L_3$, with the three generators $L_a$ of @sec-lie-algebras and real $a, b, c$, is a linear
combination; it is the general antisymmetric $3 \times 3$ matrix.
:::

Functions can be combined with coefficients exactly as columns can. Fourier series, sums of cosines and sines with
numerical coefficients, are the most important instance for physics, and they show that the candidate vectors may be
infinitely many as long as only finitely many coefficients are non-zero.

::: {#exm-combination-fourier}
#### Fourier modes

$a\cos\varphi + b\sin\varphi$ is a linear combination of the two functions $\cos\varphi$ and $\sin\varphi$; a
finite Fourier series $\sum_n (a_n \cos n\varphi + b_n \sin n\varphi)$ is a linear combination of modes.
:::

:::: {.callout-note .exercises-fold collapse="true" title="Exercises"}
Given a target vector and a family, the coefficients are the unknowns of a linear system with as many equations as
there are coordinates. The first exercise asks the reader to solve such a system by hand and then to recognise it in
Sage as a matrix equation whose columns are the given vectors.

::: {#exr-combination-solve}
#### Finding the coefficients

Write $w = (4, 7, 2)$ as a linear combination of $v_1 = (1, 2, 0)$, $v_2 = (0, 1, 1)$ and $v_4 = (0, 0, 1)$.
:::

::: {.callout-note .solution collapse="true" title="Solution"}
The coefficients solve the linear system $\lambda^1 = 4$, $2\lambda^1 + \lambda^2 = 7$, $\lambda^2 + \lambda^4 =
2$, so $\lambda = (4, -1, 3)$; in Sage the system is the matrix with columns $v_1, v_2, v_4$:

{{< sage exr-combination-solve >}}
:::

::: {.callout-tip .verification collapse="true" title="Verification"}

`la-matrix.sage`: Sage reads both sides of the goal as exact matrices (`goal.expr`), checks that `lhs - rhs` simplifies to zero, and emits the entrywise `norm_num` proof (or the closed determinant or trace formula).

For functions the same question is not a system of equations but an identity to be recognised. Here the double-angle
and triple-angle formulas of trigonometry are reread as statements that a power of a cosine or sine is a weighted sum
of a few Fourier modes.

::: {#exr-combination-fourier}
#### A trigonometric identity as a combination

Write $\cos^2\varphi$ as a linear combination of the functions $1$ and $\cos 2\varphi$, and $\sin^3\varphi$ as a
combination of $\sin\varphi$ and $\sin 3\varphi$.
:::

::: {.callout-note .solution collapse="true" title="Solution"}
From $\cos 2\varphi = 2\cos^2\varphi - 1$, $\cos^2\varphi = \tfrac12 \cdot 1 + \tfrac12 \cos 2\varphi$. From $\sin
3\varphi = 3\sin\varphi - 4\sin^3\varphi$, $\sin^3\varphi = \tfrac34 \sin\varphi - \tfrac14 \sin 3\varphi$. Every
polynomial in $\cos\varphi$ and $\sin\varphi$ is a linear combination of modes in this way.
:::

::: {.callout-tip .verification collapse="true" title="Verification"}

**Lean.**

{{< lean KaluzaKlein.LinearAlgebra.LinearCombinations.sin_cube_combination >}}

For antisymmetric matrices the coefficients can be read off directly, because each generator occupies its own pair of
entries. The task is to extract the three coefficients of a given matrix while keeping track of the sign convention
$(L_a)_{bc} = -\epsilon_{abc}$, which is easy to get backwards.

::: {#exr-combination-so3}
#### Reading off the coefficients of an antisymmetric matrix

Write the antisymmetric matrix with entries $X_{12} = -5$, $X_{13} = 2$, $X_{23} = -7$ as $a L_1 + b L_2 + c L_3$.
:::

::: {.callout-note .solution collapse="true" title="Solution"}
With $(L_a)_{bc} = -\epsilon_{abc}$, the matrix $a L_1 + b L_2 + c L_3$ has $X_{32} = a$, $X_{13} = b$, $X_{21} =
c$, so $(a, b, c) = (7, 2, 5)$:

{{< sage exr-combination-so3 >}}
:::

::: {.callout-tip .verification collapse="true" title="Verification"}
**Veriphy.** Recipe `matrix_from_goal`, certificate `la-combination-so3.sage` (`combination_so3_literal`).

**Lean.**

{{< lean KaluzaKlein.LinearAlgebra.LinearCombinations.combination_so3_literal >}}

**Sage.** The oracle of `la-combination-so3.sage` reruns the exercise's Sage solution and asserts its answer; the recipe then reads the goal and emits the proof:

```python

L3 = matrix(QQ, [[0, -1, 0], [1, 0, 0], [0, 0, 0]]); X = matrix(QQ, [[0, -5, 2], [5, 0, -7], [-2, 7, 0]])
assert X.transpose() == -X and X[2, 1] * L1 + X[0, 2] * L2 + X[1, 0] * L3 == X
print('oracle: (a, b, c) =', (X[2, 1], X[0, 2], X[1, 0]))
```

### Spans

Taking all weighted sums of a family at once produces a set, and this set is itself a subspace, the smallest one
containing the family. The following definition gives it a name; the picture is a line or a plane through the origin
swept out by the vectors drawn in it.

:::: {.statement-box}
::: {#def-span}
#### Span

The **span** of $v_1, \dots, v_k$ is the set of all their linear combinations. It is a subspace, the smallest one
containing them.
:::

::: {.callout-tip .verification collapse="true" title="Verification"}

`la-span-member.sage`: Sage solves for the coordinates of the vector in the spanning family; Lean checks the combination entry by entry.

The span of $v_1 = (1, 2, 0)$ and $v_2 = (0, 1, 1)$ is a plane through the origin; $v_3 = (1, 3, 1) = v_1 + v_2$
lies in it, so adding $v_3$ does not enlarge the span (@exr-span-dimension).

The matrix example of the previous section can now be rephrased: the whole Lie algebra $\mathfrak{so}(3)$ is the span
of three matrices. This is how a Lie algebra is usually presented, by a finite list of generators whose weighted sums
exhaust it.

::: {#exm-span-pauli}
#### Antisymmetric matrices

Every antisymmetric $3 \times 3$ matrix is a linear combination $a L_1 + b L_2 + c L_3$ of the three generators
$L_a$ of @sec-lie-algebras, so $\mathfrak{so}(3)$ is the span of $L_1, L_2, L_3$.
:::

For functions the span of finitely many modes is finite-dimensional, while the span of all of them is not. Both cases
are shown on the circle, and they prepare the count of modes carried out in the section on dimension.

::: {#exm-span-functions}
#### Fourier modes

The span of $\cos\varphi$ and $\sin\varphi$ in the functions on the circle is the two-dimensional space of first
Fourier modes $a\cos\varphi + b\sin\varphi$; the span of all $\cos n\varphi$, $\sin n\varphi$ is the
infinite-dimensional space of finite Fourier series.
:::

:::: {.callout-note .exercises-fold collapse="true" title="Exercises"}
Deciding whether a vector lies in a span is again a linear system, now one that may have no solution at all. The
exercise asks for two such decisions and for the Cartesian equation of the plane, which provides a second,
coordinate-free way of answering the same question.

::: {#exr-span-membership}
#### Membership in a span

Decide whether $(2, 5, 1)$ and $(1, 1, 1)$ lie in the span of $v_1 = (1, 2, 0)$ and $v_2 = (0, 1, 1)$, and find
the equation of the plane they span.
:::

::: {.callout-note .solution collapse="true" title="Solution"}
$(2, 5, 1) = 2 v_1 + 1 v_2$ lies in the span; $(1, 1, 1) = a v_1 + b v_2$ would need $a = 1$, $2a + b = 1$, $b = 1$,
which is contradictory. The plane is $x - \tfrac12 y + \tfrac12 z = 0$, that is, $2x - y + z = 0$:

{{< sage exr-span-membership >}}
:::

::: {.callout-tip .verification collapse="true" title="Verification"}

The geometric vocabulary of lines and planes through the origin should be matched with the algebraic notion just
defined. The reader is asked to describe the span of one, two and three vectors of $\mathbb{R}^3$ and to prove that a
dependent third vector leaves the span unchanged.

::: {#exr-span-line-plane}
#### Spans of one, two and three vectors

Describe the span of one non-zero vector of $\mathbb{R}^3$, of two vectors neither of which is a multiple of the
other, and of three vectors one of which is a combination of the other two.
:::

::: {.callout-note .solution collapse="true" title="Solution"}
One vector spans the line through the origin in its direction. Two non-proportional vectors span the plane
through the origin containing both. If $v_3 = a v_1 + b v_2$, then $\lambda^1 v_1 + \lambda^2 v_2 + \lambda^3 v_3 =
(\lambda^1 + a\lambda^3) v_1 + (\lambda^2 + b\lambda^3) v_2$, so the span of the three is the same plane as the
span of the first two.
:::

::: {.callout-tip .verification collapse="true" title="Verification"}
**Veriphy.** Test (kernel-checked, 3 instances); script `la-span-three-reduce-test.sage` (`span_three_reduce`).

**Lean.**

{{< lean KaluzaKlein.LinearAlgebra.Spans.span_three_reduce >}}

**Sage.** `la-span-three-reduce-test.sage` (kernel-checked instances): a combination of v₁, v₂, v₃ = a v₁ + b v₂ is a combination of v₁, v₂, at explicit vectors of ℝ² and ℝ³.
:::

Two different families can generate the same subspace, and proving this means expressing each family in terms of the
other. The polynomial exercise practises this with the shifted powers $(x + 1)^k$ against the plain powers $x^k$, and
also exhibits a vector that lies outside a span.

::: {#exr-span-polynomials}
#### Spans of polynomials

Show that $(x + 1)^2$ lies in the span of $1, x, x^2$, that $x^3$ does not, and that the span of $1, x, x^2$ equals
the span of $1, x + 1, (x + 1)^2$.
:::

::: {.callout-note .solution collapse="true" title="Solution"}
$(x + 1)^2 = 1 + 2x + x^2$. A combination $a + bx + cx^2$ has degree at most $2$, so $x^3$ is not one. The three
functions $1, x + 1, (x + 1)^2$ are combinations of $1, x, x^2$, and conversely $x = (x + 1) - 1$ and $x^2 = (x +
1)^2 - 2(x + 1) + 1$, so each span contains the other's generators and the spans coincide.
:::

::: {.callout-tip .verification collapse="true" title="Verification"}
**Veriphy.** Recipe `ideal_membership`, certificate `la-polynomial.sage` (`shifted_square`, `powers_from_shifted`); Test (kernel-checked, 4 instances); script `la-x-pow-not-mem-test.sage` (`X_pow_not_mem`).

### Linear independence

A span can be generated by many families, some of them wasteful. The notion defined next singles out the economical
ones, those in which no vector is a weighted sum of the others, through a single condition on the combinations that
vanish.

:::: {.statement-box}
::: {#def-linear-independence}
#### Linear independence

Vectors $v_1, \dots, v_k$ are **linearly independent** if the only linear combination equal to zero is the one
with all coefficients zero: $\lambda^i v_i = 0$ implies $\lambda^1 = \dots = \lambda^k = 0$. Otherwise they are
**linearly dependent**, and one of them is a combination of the others.
:::

::: {.callout-tip .verification collapse="true" title="Verification"}

{{< lean KaluzaKlein.Linear.f_independent_coefficients >}}

{{< lean KaluzaKlein.Linear.f_linearIndependent >}}

`la-independence.sage`: Sage finds a non-singular minor of the family (independence) or a rational relation among the vectors (dependence); Lean evaluates the minor's determinant or the relation.
:::

In the plane, the independence of two vectors is a pair of equations in two unknown coefficients. The second example
checks it for the pair $f_1, f_2$ on which the figure of the next section is built, and contrasts it with a pair of
proportional vectors.

::: {#exm-independent-basis-change}
#### Two vectors in the plane

$f_1 = (2, 1)$ and $f_2 = (1, 2)$ are independent, since $\lambda f_1 + \mu f_2 = (2\lambda + \mu, \lambda + 2\mu)$
vanishes only for $\lambda = \mu = 0$ (@fig-basis-change): from $2\lambda + \mu = 0$ and $\lambda + 2\mu = 0$,
$3\lambda = 2(2\lambda + \mu) - (\lambda + 2\mu) = 0$ and likewise $3\mu = 0$. The vectors $(2, 1)$ and $(4, 2)$ are
dependent, since $2 \cdot (2, 1) - (4, 2) = 0$.
:::

For functions a vanishing combination must vanish at every point, so evaluating at a few well-chosen points is the
standard route to independence. Dependence, by contrast, is a trigonometric identity, and $\cos^2 + \sin^2 = 1$ is the
classic one.

$1$, $\cos\varphi$, $\sin\varphi$ are independent functions on the circle (evaluate a vanishing combination at
$\varphi = 0, \pi/2, \pi$); $\cos^2\varphi$, $\sin^2\varphi$ and $1$ are dependent, since $\cos^2 + \sin^2 - 1 = 0$.
:::

The evaluation trick of the last example deserves to be carried out in full. The exercise asks for the three equations
that force the coefficients of $1$, $\cos\varphi$, $\sin\varphi$ to vanish, and for the explicit relation that makes
$1$, $\cos^2\varphi$, $\sin^2\varphi$ dependent.

::: {#exr-independence-functions}
#### Independent functions

Show that $1$, $\cos\varphi$, $\sin\varphi$ are linearly independent functions on the circle and that
$1$, $\cos^2\varphi$, $\sin^2\varphi$ are not.
:::

::: {.callout-note .solution collapse="true" title="Solution"}
If $a + b\cos\varphi + c\sin\varphi = 0$ for all $\varphi$, evaluating at $\varphi = 0, \pi, \pi/2$ gives
$a + b = 0$, $a - b = 0$, $a + c = 0$, so $a = b = c = 0$. For the second family, $1 - \cos^2\varphi - \sin^2\varphi
= 0$ is a vanishing combination with non-zero coefficients.
:::

`la-trig-pythagoras.sage`: Sage confirms $\cos^2 x + \sin^2 x - 1 = 0$ before the rewrite by `Real.cos_sq_add_sin_sq` is emitted.

`la-independence-eval.sage`: Sage evaluates the family exactly at points (values, matrix entries or coefficients) and picks those giving a non-singular matrix; Lean checks its determinant.

`la-dependence-functions.sage`: Sage finds the relation $1 - \cos^2 - \sin^2 = 0$ as a kernel vector of the coefficients in $\cos x$ and the multiple of $\cos^2 + \sin^2 = 1$ that closes it.
:::

When there are as many vectors as coordinates, a single number decides the matter: the determinant of the matrix with
the vectors as columns. The test is applied to two families in $\mathbb{R}^4$, and Sage is asked for the dependence
relation in the case where the determinant vanishes.

::: {#exr-independence-determinant}
#### Independence by a determinant

Use the determinant to decide whether $(1, 0, 1, 0)$, $(0, 1, 0, 1)$, $(1, 1, 0, 0)$, $(0, 0, 1, -1)$ are
independent in $\mathbb{R}^4$, and whether the family with the last vector replaced by $(0, 0, 1, 1)$ is; find the
dependence relation when there is one.
:::

::: {.callout-note .solution collapse="true" title="Solution"}
$n$ vectors of $\mathbb{R}^n$ are independent exactly when the matrix with these columns has non-zero determinant
(its kernel is then $\{0\}$). The first family has determinant $2$; the second has determinant $0$ and the relation
$v_1 + v_2 - v_3 - v_4 = 0$:

{{< sage exr-independence-determinant >}}
:::

::: {.callout-tip .verification collapse="true" title="Verification"}
**Veriphy.** Recipe `matrix_from_goal`, certificate `la-independence-determinant.sage` (`det_family_F`, `det_family_F_rows`, `det_family_G`, `family_G_relation`); Recipe `independence`, certificate `la-independence.sage` (`family_F_independent`, `family_G_dependent`).

**Lean.**

{{< lean KaluzaKlein.LinearAlgebra.LinearIndependence.family_F_independent >}}

{{< lean KaluzaKlein.LinearAlgebra.LinearIndependence.det_family_G >}}

{{< lean KaluzaKlein.LinearAlgebra.LinearIndependence.family_G_dependent >}}

**Sage.** The oracle of `la-independence-determinant.sage` reruns the exercise's Sage solution and asserts its answer; the recipe then reads the goal and emits the proof:

```python
F = [vector(QQ, [1, 0, 1, 0]), vector(QQ, [0, 1, 0, 1]), vector(QQ, [1, 1, 0, 0]), vector(QQ, [0, 0, 1, -1])]
G = [vector(QQ, [1, 0, 1, 0]), vector(QQ, [0, 1, 0, 1]), vector(QQ, [1, 1, 0, 0]), vector(QQ, [0, 0, 1, 1])]
assert matrix(QQ, F).transpose().det() == 2 and matrix(QQ, G).transpose().det() == 0
assert (QQ ^ 4).linear_dependence(G) == [vector(QQ, [1, 1, -1, -1])]
print('oracle: det F = 2, det G = 0, relation (1, 1, -1, -1)')
```

`la-independence.sage`: Sage finds a non-singular minor of the family (independence) or a rational relation among the vectors (dependence); Lean evaluates the minor's determinant or the relation.
:::

An independent family can be enlarged by any vector outside its span, and this is the step by which bases are built
one vector at a time. The exercise asks for the proof, a short argument by contradiction on the coefficient of the new
vector.

::: {#exr-independence-extend}
#### Extending an independent family

Prove that if $v_1, \dots, v_k$ are independent and $v$ is not in their span, then $v_1, \dots, v_k, v$ are
independent.
:::

::: {.callout-note .solution collapse="true" title="Solution"}
Suppose $\lambda^i v_i + \mu v = 0$. If $\mu \neq 0$, then $v = -\mu^{-1}\lambda^i v_i$ lies in the span,
contradicting the hypothesis; so $\mu = 0$, and then $\lambda^i v_i = 0$ forces every $\lambda^i = 0$ by the
independence of the $v_i$. Repeating the step builds a basis from any independent family, the argument behind
@def-basis.
:::

::: {.callout-tip .verification collapse="true" title="Verification"}
**Veriphy.** Test (kernel-checked, 3 instances); script `la-extend-independent-test.sage` (`extend_independent`).

**Lean.**

{{< lean KaluzaKlein.LinearAlgebra.LinearIndependence.extend_independent >}}

**Sage.** `la-extend-independent-test.sage` (kernel-checked instances): an independent family extended by a vector outside its span, at n = 0, 1, 2 in ℚ² and ℚ³: the extended family has a non-singular minor (checked by evaluation).
:::

### Bases

![One vector, two bases: $v = (5, 4)$ has coordinates $(5, 4)$ in the standard basis $e_1, e_2$ (grey grid) and
$(2, 1)$ in the basis $f_1 = (2, 1)$, $f_2 = (1, 2)$ (blue grid). Generated by `figures/basis_change.sage` with
Sage's `VectorSpace`.](figures/basis_change.svg){#fig-basis-change width=55%}

{{< interactive basis_change 520 >}}

An independent family that also spans the whole space is the ideal coordinate system: every vector is a weighted sum
of it in exactly one way. The definition names such families and their coefficients; the figure above shows one vector
read off two different grids.

:::: {.statement-box}
::: {#def-basis}
#### Basis

A **basis** of $V$ is a linearly independent family $e_1, \dots, e_n$ that spans $V$. Every vector is then a
unique linear combination $v = v^i e_i$, and the numbers $v^i$ are the **coordinates** (or **components**) of $v$
in the basis.
:::

::: {.callout-tip .verification collapse="true" title="Verification"}
**Veriphy.** Recipe `witness`, certificate `witness.sage` (`coordinates_f_exist`); Recipe `matrix_from_goal`, certificate `la-matrix-named.sage` (`fBasis_coords`).

**Lean.**

{{< lean KaluzaKlein.Linear.coordinates_f_exist >}}

{{< lean KaluzaKlein.LinearAlgebra.Bases.fBasis_coords >}}

`la-matrix-named.sage`: Sage reads both sides of the goal as exact matrices or vectors (named matrices through their literal definitions) and checks that `lhs - rhs` is zero; Lean checks it entry by entry.
:::
::::

:::: {.callout-note .examples-fold collapse="true" title="Examples"}
The first instance is the grid of the coordinate axes themselves. Its coordinates are simply the entries of the
column, which is why this basis is invisible in most computations and why one forgets that a choice was made.

::: {#exm-basis-standard}
#### The standard basis

$e_1 = (1, 0, \dots, 0), \dots, e_n = (0, \dots, 0, 1)$ is the standard basis of $\mathbb{R}^n$, and the
coordinates of $(x^1, \dots, x^n)$ are the $x^i$ themselves.
:::

::: {.callout-tip .verification collapse="true" title="Verification"}

:::

The second grid of the figure is skewed. The example gives the coordinates of $v = (5, 4)$ in it, which differ from
its standard entries, and draws the moral that a change of coordinates is nothing but a change of basis.

::: {#exm-basis-f}
#### A different basis of the plane

$f_1 = (2, 1)$, $f_2 = (1, 2)$ is a basis of $\mathbb{R}^2$, and $v = (5, 4) = 2 f_1 + 1 f_2$ has coordinates
$(2, 1)$ in it (@fig-basis-change, @prp-coordinates-f). The same vector has different coordinates in different bases;
this is the whole content of "coordinate transformations". In the interactive figure, hovering a node of the blue
grid shows both sets of coordinates.
:::

::: {#exr-basis-coordinates}
#### Checking a basis and finding coordinates

Show that $b_1 = (1, 1, 0)$, $b_2 = (0, 1, 1)$, $b_3 = (1, 0, 1)$ is a basis of $\mathbb{R}^3$ and find the
coordinates of $(2, 3, 4)$ in it.

::: {.callout-note .solution collapse="true" title="Solution"}
The matrix with columns $b_j$ has determinant $2 \neq 0$, so the three vectors are independent, and three
independent vectors in a three-dimensional space span it. The coordinates solve $C\lambda = (2, 3, 4)$, giving
$(\tfrac12, \tfrac52, \tfrac32)$:

{{< sage exr-basis-coordinates >}}

For the matrix example a proof is called for rather than a computation: the three generators span and are independent.
The argument runs through the three entries above the diagonal of an antisymmetric matrix, which determine it
completely.

::: {#exr-basis-so3}
#### The generators form a basis

Prove that $L_1, L_2, L_3$ with $(L_a)_{bc} = -\epsilon_{abc}$ form a basis of the antisymmetric $3 \times 3$
matrices.
:::

::: {.callout-note .solution collapse="true" title="Solution"}
An antisymmetric matrix is determined by its three entries above the diagonal, $X_{12}, X_{13}, X_{23}$, and
$a L_1 + b L_2 + c L_3$ has $(X_{12}, X_{13}, X_{23}) = (-c, b, -a)$. Any triple of entries is reached (spanning),
and the zero triple only by $a = b = c = 0$ (independence); @exr-combination-so3 reads off the coefficients for one
matrix.
:::

A basis can be chosen so that the coordinates of a polynomial are its values at chosen points rather than its monomial
coefficients. The exercise constructs the simplest such basis, for degree one, and reads the coordinates of $3x + 2$
off its values at $0$ and $1$.

::: {#exr-basis-lagrange}
#### A basis adapted to evaluation

Show that $\ell_0(x) = 1 - x$ and $\ell_1(x) = x$ form a basis of the polynomials of degree at most $1$, and find
the coordinates of $p(x) = 3x + 2$ in it.
:::

::: {.callout-note .solution collapse="true" title="Solution"}
$a\ell_0 + b\ell_1 = a + (b - a)x$ vanishes only if $a = 0$ and $b = a = 0$, and $c + dx = c\,\ell_0 + (c + d)\ell_1$
shows spanning. Since $\ell_0(0) = 1, \ell_0(1) = 0$ and $\ell_1(0) = 0, \ell_1(1) = 1$, the coordinates of $p$ are
its values $(p(0), p(1)) = (2, 5)$: $3x + 2 = 2(1 - x) + 5x$. Bases adapted to evaluation are the Lagrange bases of
interpolation.
:::

::: {.callout-tip .verification collapse="true" title="Verification"}

### Dimension

The number of vectors in a basis does not depend on which basis is chosen, and this number is the first invariant of a
vector space. The definition records it; the picture is the number of independent directions available in the space.

:::: {.statement-box}
::: {#def-dimension}
#### Dimension

All bases of $V$ have the same number of elements, the **dimension** $\dim V$. A vector space with a finite basis
is **finite-dimensional**.
:::

A span's dimension is not the number of generators but the number of independent ones among them. The example returns
to the dependent triple of $\mathbb{R}^3$, whose span is only a plane.

::: {#exm-dimension-span}
#### Dimension of a span

The span of $(1, 2, 0)$, $(0, 1, 1)$, $(1, 3, 1)$ has dimension $2$, not $3$, because of the dependence relation
(@exr-span-dimension); the dimension of a span is the number of independent vectors among the generators.
:::

::: {#exr-span-dimension}
#### Span and dimension

With Sage's `VectorSpace`, find the dimension of the span of $(1, 2, 0)$, $(0, 1, 1)$, $(1, 3, 1)$ in
$\mathbb{Q}^3$, the dependence relation among them, and the coordinates of $(2, 5, 1)$ in the basis $(1, 2, 0)$,
$(0, 1, 1)$, $(0, 0, 1)$.
:::

::: {.callout-note .solution collapse="true" title="Solution"}
The span is a plane (dimension $2$) because $v_3 = v_1 + v_2$; replacing $v_3$ by $(0, 0, 1)$ gives a basis of
$\mathbb{Q}^3$, in which $(2, 5, 1) = 2 v_1 + 1 v_2 + 0 v_4$:

{{< sage exr-span-dimension >}}
:::

Splitting a matrix into symmetric and antisymmetric parts gives two subspaces whose dimensions must add up to $n^2$.
The exercise asks for both counts and for the reason the sum comes out right, which is a direct-sum decomposition.

::: {#exr-dimension-symmetric}
#### Symmetric and antisymmetric matrices

Find the dimensions of the symmetric and of the antisymmetric $n \times n$ matrices and check that they add up to
$n^2$.
:::

::: {.callout-note .solution collapse="true" title="Solution"}
A symmetric matrix is determined by its entries on and above the diagonal, $n + (n^2 - n)/2 = n(n + 1)/2$ of
them; an antisymmetric one by the entries strictly above the diagonal, $n(n - 1)/2$ of them. The sum is $n^2$, as
it must be: every matrix is uniquely $\tfrac12(A + A^{\mathsf{T}}) + \tfrac12(A - A^{\mathsf{T}})$, so the space of
all matrices is the direct sum of the two subspaces (@exr-symmetric-tensors-dim computes the counts for small $n$).
:::

Counting the trigonometric modes up to a fixed order gives the dimension of a space of trigonometric polynomials. The
exercise contrasts the count $2N + 1$ for sines and cosines with the count for powers of a cosine, which generate only
the even modes.

::: {#exr-dimension-fourier}
#### Fourier modes of bounded order

Find the dimension of the span of $1, \cos\varphi, \sin\varphi, \dots, \cos N\varphi, \sin N\varphi$, and of the
span of $\cos^k\varphi$ for $k = 0, \dots, N$.
:::

::: {.callout-note .solution collapse="true" title="Solution"}
The $2N + 1$ modes are independent (a vanishing combination has zero Fourier coefficients, by integrating against
each mode as in @exr-functional-integration), so the dimension is $2N + 1$. The powers $\cos^k\varphi$, $k \leq N$,
are also independent (a vanishing polynomial in $\cos\varphi$ of degree $\leq N$ has infinitely many roots), so
that span has dimension $N + 1$; it is the subspace of even modes $1, \cos\varphi, \dots, \cos N\varphi$.
:::

::: {.callout-tip .verification collapse="true" title="Verification"}

The two simplest dimension counts are those of the coordinate space and of the square matrices. The proposition
records them for size three, where every later example of this chapter lives.

:::: {.callout-note .examples-fold collapse="true" title="Examples"}
The first count is an instance of a general fact about functions on a finite set. A column of $n$ numbers is a
function on $\{1, \dots, n\}$, and the functions that are $1$ at one point and $0$ elsewhere form a basis.

::: {#exm-dim-lean-pi}
#### Functions on a finite set

The real functions on a finite set $X$ form a vector space of dimension $|X|$: the functions $\delta_x$, equal to
$1$ at $x$ and $0$ elsewhere, form a basis, since $f = \sum_x f(x)\, \delta_x$. For $X = \{1, 2, 3\}$ this is
$\dim \mathbb{R}^3 = 3$; the functions on a five-element set form a five-dimensional space.
:::

::: {.callout-tip .verification collapse="true" title="Verification"}
**Veriphy.** Test (kernel-checked, 4 instances); script `la-finrank-functions-test.sage` (`finrank_functions`); Recipe `dimension`, certificate `la-dim-product.sage` (`finrank_functions_five`).

**Lean.**

{{< lean KaluzaKlein.LinearAlgebra.VectorSpaceResults.finrank_functions >}}

{{< lean KaluzaKlein.LinearAlgebra.VectorSpaceResults.finrank_functions_five >}}

`la-dim-product.sage`: Sage evaluates the product formula for the dimension; Lean applies mathlib's finrank formulas for coordinate spaces, matrices, tensor products and duals.
:::

The second count works the same way once a matrix is seen as a function of two indices. The example spells out the
product of the two index ranges, the first time in this chapter that a dimension is seen to multiply.

::: {#exm-dim-lean-matrix}
#### Matrices as functions of two indices

A $3 \times 3$ matrix is a function of a row index and a column index, so the matrices are the functions on the
$3 \cdot 3 = 9$ index pairs and have dimension $9$; the $2 \times 3$ matrices have dimension $2 \cdot 3 = 6$. The
dimension of a space of matrices is the product of the index ranges.
:::

A single linear condition on a space of matrices lowers its dimension by one. The trace is such a condition, and
the matrices it annihilates form the Lie algebra of the special linear group.

::: {#exm-dim-sage}
#### Traceless matrices

The trace $A \mapsto A_{11} + A_{22} + A_{33}$ is a non-zero linear functional on the $3 \times 3$ matrices, so its
kernel, the traceless matrices, has dimension $9 - 1 = 8$ by rank-nullity (@def-linear-map).
:::

::: {.callout-tip .verification collapse="true" title="Verification"}
**Veriphy.** Recipe `dimension`, certificate `la-dim-ker.sage` (`finrank_traceless`).

**Lean.**

{{< lean KaluzaKlein.LinearAlgebra.VectorSpaceResults.finrank_traceless >}}

**Sage.** `la-dim-ker.sage`: Sage finds a vector the functional sends to $1$; Lean concludes by rank-nullity (`Veriphy.Linear.finrank_ker_add_one`).
:::

:::: {.callout-note .exercises-fold collapse="true" title="Exercises"}
The product formula for matrices applies to other shapes and other fields of scalars. The exercise asks for three
counts, and the last two show that the dimension of a complex space depends on whether one counts over $\mathbb{R}$
or over $\mathbb{C}$.

::: {#exr-dim-matrix-lean}
#### Dimensions over $\mathbb{R}$ and over $\mathbb{C}$

Find the dimension of the $2 \times 3$ real matrices, of the $2 \times 2$ complex matrices as a complex vector space,
and of the same matrices as a real vector space.
:::

::: {.callout-note .solution collapse="true" title="Solution"}
$2 \cdot 3 \cdot \dim_{\mathbb{R}} \mathbb{R} = 6$, and $2 \cdot 2 \cdot \dim_{\mathbb{C}} \mathbb{C} = 4$. As a
real vector space the complex $2 \times 2$ matrices have dimension $8$, since $\dim_{\mathbb{R}} \mathbb{C} = 2$:
the dimension depends on the field of scalars.
:::

A plane through the origin has dimension two, but a basis of it still has to be found, and more than one choice is
possible. The exercise asks for two different bases of the plane $x + y + z = 0$ and compares them with the
echelonised basis that Sage returns.

#### Dimension of a plane

Find the dimension of the plane $x + y + z = 0$ in $\mathbb{R}^3$ and two different bases of it.

The plane is the kernel of the row $(1, 1, 1)$; two independent solutions, such as $(1, -1, 0)$ and $(0, 1, -1)$,

For two subspaces, the dimensions of their sum and of their intersection are tied together by a formula. The exercise
verifies it for two planes in $\mathbb{R}^3$, which meet in a line and together fill the whole space.

::: {#exr-dim-sum-intersection}
#### Dimension of a sum and an intersection

For two planes $U, W$ through the origin in $\mathbb{R}^3$, verify $\dim(U + W) = \dim U + \dim W - \dim(U \cap W)$
with $U = \{z = 0\}$ and $W = \operatorname{span}\{(1, 2, 0), (0, 1, 1)\}$.
:::

::: {.callout-note .solution collapse="true" title="Solution"}
Two distinct planes through the origin meet in a line and together span the space: $3 = 2 + 2 - 1$. The
intersection is the line through $(1, 2, 0)$, the only direction of $W$ with $z = 0$:

{{< sage exr-dim-sum-intersection >}}
:::

The coordinates of $(5, 4)$ in the basis $f$ were read off the figure; the second proposition records them. They are

$(5, 4) = 2 f_1 + 1 f_2$ for $f_1 = (2, 1)$, $f_2 = (1, 2)$: the coordinates of $(5, 4)$ in the basis $f$ are
$(2, 1)$.

:::: {.callout-note .examples-fold collapse="true" title="Examples"}
The two coordinates solve a pair of linear equations, and doing it by hand is the most direct route. One
elimination step recovers $a = 2$ and $b = 1$.

::: {#exm-coords-system}
#### Solving the system by hand

$a f_1 + b f_2 = (5, 4)$ means $2a + b = 5$ and $a + 2b = 4$; subtracting twice the second from the first gives
$-3b = -3$, so $b = 1$ and $a = 2$.
:::

::: {.callout-tip .verification collapse="true" title="Verification"}
**Veriphy.** Recipe `ideal_membership`, certificate `ideal_membership.sage` (`coords_system`).

**Lean.**

{{< lean KaluzaKlein.LinearAlgebra.VectorSpaceResults.coords_system >}}

**Sage.** `ideal_membership.sage`: Sage writes `lhs - rhs` as a combination of the hypotheses (`goal.poly.lift(...)`, a Gröbner-basis computation); the cofactors are the coefficients of the emitted `linear_combination`.
:::

A solution found by any method can be checked by substituting it back, and the determinant of the system decides
whether it is the only one. The second example does both for the coordinates of $(5, 4)$.

::: {#exm-coords-witness}
#### Checking the coordinates

Substituting $a = 2$, $b = 1$ gives $2 \cdot 2 + 1 = 5$ and $2 + 2 \cdot 1 = 4$, so $2 f_1 + f_2 = (5, 4)$. The
solution is unique because the matrix of the system, with columns $f_1, f_2$, has determinant $2 \cdot 2 - 1 \cdot 1
= 3 \neq 0$.
:::

The inverse-matrix formula for coordinates deserves both a proof and a worked instance. The exercise asks for both,
and the inverse for the basis $f$ turns out to carry the dual basis of the next section in its rows.

::: {#exr-coords-inverse-matrix}
#### Coordinates by the inverse matrix

Show that the coordinates of $v$ in a basis $f_1, \dots, f_n$ of $\mathbb{R}^n$ are $F^{-1} v$, where $F$ is the
matrix with columns $f_j$, and compute $F^{-1}$ for $f = ((2, 1), (1, 2))$.
:::

::: {.callout-note .solution collapse="true" title="Solution"}
$v = \lambda^j f_j$ is the matrix product $v = F\lambda$, and $F$ is invertible because its columns are
independent, so $\lambda = F^{-1} v$. For $F = \begin{pmatrix} 2 & 1 \\ 1 & 2 \end{pmatrix}$, $\det F = 3$ and
$F^{-1} = \tfrac13 \begin{pmatrix} 2 & -1 \\ -1 & 2 \end{pmatrix}$, whose rows are the dual basis of
@exm-dual-f; $F^{-1}(5, 4) = (2, 1)$.
:::

::: {.callout-tip .verification collapse="true" title="Verification"}

## Linear maps and dual spaces {#sec-linear-maps-dual}

A linear map is a map between vector spaces that respects addition and scaling; its matrix is the array of
numbers that every computation in these lectures manipulates. The linear maps to the real numbers, the covectors,
form the dual space, and the dual basis turns coordinates into functionals. Four definitions and two propositions,
on a kernel vector and on the dual basis of $f$.

### Linear maps

A map between vector spaces is useful only if it respects the two operations, and the maps that do are the subject of
this section. The definition also names the kernel and the image, states the rank-nullity count that ties them to the
dimension, and explains how a matrix arises once bases are fixed.

:::: {.statement-box}
::: {#def-linear-map}
#### Linear map

A map $L : V \to W$ between vector spaces is **linear** if $L(v + w) = L(v) + L(w)$ and $L(\lambda v) = \lambda
L(v)$. Its **kernel** $\ker L = \{v : L(v) = 0\}$ and **image** $L(V)$ are subspaces, and $\dim \ker L + \dim L(V)
= \dim V$ (**rank-nullity**). In bases $e_j$ of $V$ and $f_i$ of $W$, $L(e_j) = L^i{}_j f_i$ defines the **matrix**
$L^i{}_j$ of $L$, and $L(v)^i = L^i{}_j v^j$.
:::

::: {.callout-tip .verification collapse="true" title="Verification"}

Rotations and the derivative are linear maps of a different flavour: one is a bijection of $\mathbb{R}^3$, the other
lowers the degree of polynomials and annihilates the constants. The example records the kernel of each and the rank of
the derivative.

::: {#exm-linear-rotation}
#### Rotations and derivatives

A rotation $R \in SO(3)$ is a linear bijection of $\mathbb{R}^3$ with kernel $\{0\}$. The derivative $f \mapsto f'$
is a linear map of the polynomials of degree at most $2$ to those of degree at most $1$, with kernel the constants
and rank $2$ (@exr-matrix-of-derivative).
:::

To see what linearity excludes, a few familiar maps that are not linear are listed. Translations, squares and the
parametrisation of a circle all fail, and the example closes with the consequence that makes linear maps tractable:
their values on a basis determine them.

::: {#exm-linear-not}
#### Non-linear maps

$x \mapsto x + 1$ is not linear ($L(0) \neq 0$), nor is $x \mapsto x^2$; the parametrisation $\varphi \mapsto
(\cos\varphi, \sin\varphi)$ of the circle is not linear either. Linearity is a strong condition: a linear map is
determined by its values on a basis.
:::

:::: {.callout-note .exercises-fold collapse="true" title="Exercises"}
Testing linearity means checking additivity and homogeneity, or finding a single input that breaks one of them. Four
maps are presented, two on the plane and two on functions, and the reader should name the specific counterexample for
each one that fails.

::: {#exr-linear-check}
#### Which maps are linear?

Decide which of the following maps are linear: $(x, y) \mapsto (x + y, xy)$; $(x, y) \mapsto (2x - y, 0)$;
$f \mapsto \int_0^1 f(x)\,dx$ on polynomials; $f \mapsto f^2$ on functions.
:::

::: {.callout-note .solution collapse="true" title="Solution"}
The second and third are linear: $2(x + x') - (y + y') = (2x - y) + (2x' - y')$, and the integral of a sum is the
sum of the integrals. The first is not, because of the product $xy$: $L(2(1, 1)) = (4, 4) \neq 2L(1, 1) = (4, 2)$.
The fourth is not: $(f + g)^2 \neq f^2 + g^2$ in general.
:::

::: {.callout-tip .verification collapse="true" title="Verification"}

A linear map between function spaces acquires a matrix once bases are chosen, and the derivative on quadratics is the
smallest interesting case. The exercise asks for its $2 \times 3$ matrix and reads kernel and rank off the columns.

::: {#exr-matrix-of-derivative}
#### The matrix of the derivative

Write the matrix of $f \mapsto f'$ from the polynomials of degree $\leq 2$ to those of degree $\leq 1$ in the
bases $1, x, x^2$ and $1, x$, and read off its kernel and rank.
:::

::: {.callout-note .solution collapse="true" title="Solution"}
$1 \mapsto 0$, $x \mapsto 1$, $x^2 \mapsto 2x$, so the columns are $(0, 0)$, $(1, 0)$, $(0, 2)$ and the matrix is
$\begin{pmatrix} 0 & 1 & 0 \\ 0 & 0 & 2 \end{pmatrix}$. Its rank is $2$ (the map is surjective) and its kernel
is the span of the first basis vector, the constants, of dimension $3 - 2 = 1$.

:::

### Linear functionals

![Level lines of the linear functional $\alpha = 2x + y$ on $\mathbb{R}^2$: the black line is the kernel, and
$\alpha(v)$ counts the level lines a vector crosses. Generated by
`figures/level_sets.sage`.](figures/level_sets.svg){#fig-level-sets width=50%}

The simplest target for a linear map is the real line itself, and linear maps into it are important enough to deserve
their own name. The figure above shows one on the plane: its level lines are parallel, and its kernel is the one line
among them that passes through the origin.

:::: {.statement-box}
::: {#def-linear-functional}
#### Linear functional

A **linear functional** (or **covector**) on $V$ is a linear map $\alpha : V \to \mathbb{R}$.
:::

$\mathbb{R}^n$.

Every linear functional on $\mathbb{R}^n$ is given by a row of numbers, and evaluating it is a row-times-column
product. The example fixes the convention used from here on: columns are vectors, rows are covectors.

::: {#exm-functional-row}
#### Row vectors

Every linear functional on $\mathbb{R}^n$ is $v \mapsto a_i v^i$ for a unique row $(a_1, \dots, a_n)$: columns are
vectors, rows are covectors. The pairing $a_i v^i$ is the matrix product of a row with a column.
:::

::: {.callout-tip .verification collapse="true" title="Verification"}

**Sage.** `la-functional-is-row-test.sage` (kernel-checked instances): α(v) = Σ v^i α(e_i) for the zero functional, a coordinate and a row functional, by evaluation.
:::

On function spaces the natural functionals are evaluation at a point and integration over the domain. The example
records both and points ahead to the differential of a function, the functional on tangent vectors that @sec-one-forms
studies.

::: {#exm-functional-evaluation}
#### Evaluation and integration

On the functions on the circle, $f \mapsto f(0)$ and $f \mapsto \int_0^{2\pi} f(\varphi)\, d\varphi$ are linear
functionals; the differential $df_p$ of a function at a point is a linear functional on the tangent space
(@sec-one-forms).
:::

The level-set picture of the figure extends to three dimensions, where the kernel of a functional is a plane and the
level sets are parallel planes. The exercise asks for them and for the dimension of the kernel, obtained by
rank-nullity.

::: {#exr-functional-kernel}
#### Kernel and level sets of a functional

For $\alpha(x, y, z) = 3x - y + 2z$ on $\mathbb{R}^3$, describe the kernel and the level sets $\alpha = c$, and
find the dimension of the kernel.
:::

::: {.callout-note .solution collapse="true" title="Solution"}
The kernel is the plane $3x - y + 2z = 0$ through the origin, of dimension $3 - 1 = 2$ by rank-nullity (the image
of a non-zero functional is all of $\mathbb{R}$, rank $1$). The level sets are the parallel planes $3x - y + 2z =
c$, translates of the kernel; the row $(3, -1, 2)$ is normal to all of them.
:::

The claim that rows exhaust the functionals on $\mathbb{R}^n$ was only asserted; the exercise asks for the proof. The
argument sets $a_i = \alpha(e_i)$ and uses linearity, and the uniqueness part shows that a functional is determined by
its values on a basis.

::: {#exr-functional-rows}
#### Every functional is a row

Prove that every linear functional $\alpha$ on $\mathbb{R}^n$ is of the form $v \mapsto a_i v^i$, and that the row
$(a_i)$ is unique.
:::

::: {.callout-note .solution collapse="true" title="Solution"}
Set $a_i = \alpha(e_i)$. By linearity, $\alpha(v) = \alpha(v^i e_i) = v^i \alpha(e_i) = a_i v^i$. If also $\alpha(v)
= b_i v^i$ for all $v$, then evaluating at $v = e_j$ gives $a_j = b_j$. A linear functional is therefore determined
by its $n$ values on a basis, like any linear map.
:::

Integration over the circle is a functional on the Fourier modes, and its row is particularly simple. The exercise
evaluates it on a few modes, checks linearity, and finds that every non-constant mode lies in its kernel, the fact
behind the orthogonality of Fourier modes.

::: {#exr-functional-integration}
#### The integral as a functional

Compute the functional $I(f) = \int_0^{2\pi} f(\varphi)\, d\varphi$ on $1$, $\cos\varphi$, $\sin 2\varphi$ and
$\cos^2\varphi$, check its linearity on two combinations, and write its row on the basis $1, \cos\varphi,
\sin\varphi$.
:::

::: {.callout-note .solution collapse="true" title="Solution"}
$I(1) = 2\pi$, $I(\cos\varphi) = I(\sin 2\varphi) = 0$, $I(\cos^2\varphi) = \pi$; its row on $(1, \cos\varphi,
\sin\varphi)$ is $(2\pi, 0, 0)$, so its kernel contains every non-constant mode:

{{< sage exr-functional-integration >}}
:::

### The dual space

The linear functionals on $V$ can themselves be added and rescaled, so they form a vector space of their own. The
definition names this space and records that it has the same dimension as $V$; the picture is the rows standing beside
the columns.

:::: {.statement-box}
::: {#def-dual-space}
#### Dual space

The **dual space** $V^*$ is the vector space of all linear functionals on $V$, with $(\alpha + \beta)(v) = \alpha(v) +
\beta(v)$ and $(\lambda\alpha)(v) = \lambda\,\alpha(v)$; $\dim V^* = \dim V$.
:::

::: {.callout-tip .verification collapse="true" title="Verification"}
**Veriphy.** Test (kernel-checked, 4 instances); script `la-finrank-dual-test.sage` (`finrank_dual`).

**Lean.**

{{< lean KaluzaKlein.LinearAlgebra.DualSpace.finrank_dual >}}

**Sage.** `la-finrank-dual-test.sage` (kernel-checked instances): dim V* = dim V at V = ℚ⁰, ℚ², ℚ³ and ℚ, by the finrank formulas.
:::
::::

:::: {.callout-note .examples-fold collapse="true" title="Examples"}
For coordinate space the dual is the space of rows. The example stresses that although rows and columns have the same
dimension they are different kinds of object, which is what the position of an index will keep track of.

::: {#exm-dual-space-rows}
#### Rows

The dual of $\mathbb{R}^n$ (columns) is the space of rows $(a_1, \dots, a_n)$, acting by $a_i v^i$; it has
dimension $n$, like $\mathbb{R}^n$ itself, but a row and a column are different kinds of object.
:::

::: {.callout-tip .verification collapse="true" title="Verification"}
**Veriphy.** Test (kernel-checked, 3 instances); script `la-finrank-dual-rn-test.sage` (`finrank_dual_rn`).

**Lean.**

{{< lean KaluzaKlein.LinearAlgebra.DualSpace.finrank_dual_rn >}}

**Sage.** `la-finrank-dual-rn-test.sage` (kernel-checked instances): dim (ℝⁿ)* = n at seeded n (0 and 1 among them).
:::

On a manifold the dual of each tangent space is the cotangent space, the home of differentials. The example makes the
connection now so that the one-forms of @sec-one-forms are recognised as covectors when they appear.

::: {#exm-dual-space-cotangent}
#### Cotangent spaces

The dual of the tangent space $T_pM$ of a manifold is the **cotangent space** $T_p^*M$, where differentials of
functions and components of one-forms live (@sec-one-forms).
:::

::: {.callout-tip .verification collapse="true" title="Verification"}
**Veriphy.** Test (kernel-checked, 3 instances); script `la-finrank-cotangent-test.sage` (`finrank_cotangent`).

**Lean.**

{{< lean KaluzaKlein.LinearAlgebra.DualSpace.finrank_cotangent >}}

**Sage.** `la-finrank-cotangent-test.sage` (kernel-checked instances): the cotangent space of the model ℝⁿ at a point has dimension n, at n = 0, 2, 3.
:::

Taking the dual twice brings one back to the original space, at least in finite dimension. The example explains how a
vector acts on covectors, which is the reason vectors and covectors enter the tensor calculus on an equal footing.

::: {#exm-dual-space-dual-dual}
#### The double dual

The dual of $V^*$ is $V$ again for finite-dimensional $V$: a vector $v$ acts on covectors by $\alpha \mapsto
\alpha(v)$, and every linear functional on $V^*$ is of this form. This is why vectors and covectors are treated
symmetrically in the tensor calculus of @sec-tensor-products.
:::

The operations in the dual space are the operations on rows, and this is best seen on numbers. The exercise evaluates
sums and multiples of two functionals on a fixed vector and checks that the coordinate functionals span the dual.

::: {#exr-dual-rows}
#### Operations on functionals

For $\alpha = (2, 1, 0)$ and $\beta = (1, -1, 3)$ as rows on $\mathbb{R}^3$, compute $\alpha(v)$, $\beta(v)$,
$(\alpha + \beta)(v)$ and $(4\alpha)(v)$ for $v = (1, 2, 3)$, and check that the coordinate functionals span the
dual.

::: {.callout-note .solution collapse="true" title="Solution"}
$\alpha(v) = 4$, $\beta(v) = 8$, $(\alpha + \beta)(v) = 12$, $(4\alpha)(v) = 16$: the sum and the multiple of
functionals are the sum and the multiple of their rows. $\alpha = 2e^1 + e^2$ is a combination of the coordinate
functionals, which span the row space:

{{< sage exr-dual-rows >}}
:::

The claim $\dim V^* = \dim V$ needs a basis of the dual, and constructing one is the content of this exercise. The
functionals that return coordinates do the job, and the proof is a preview of the dual basis defined in the next
section.

::: {#exr-dual-dimension}
#### The dual has the same dimension

Prove that $\dim V^* = \dim V$ for finite-dimensional $V$ by exhibiting a basis of $V^*$.
:::

::: {.callout-note .solution collapse="true" title="Solution"}
Let $e_1, \dots, e_n$ be a basis and $e^i$ the functionals with $e^i(e_j) = \delta^i_j$ (they exist, since a linear
map is determined by its values on a basis). They span: $\alpha = \alpha(e_i) e^i$, because both sides agree on
every $e_j$. They are independent: if $\lambda_i e^i = 0$, evaluating at $e_j$ gives $\lambda_j = 0$. So $V^*$ has a
basis of $n$ elements; this is the dual basis of @def-dual-basis.
:::

The identification of $V$ with its double dual is made precise by an explicit map, evaluation. The exercise asks for
its linearity and injectivity, and rank-nullity then upgrades injectivity to an isomorphism.

::: {#exr-dual-double}
#### Into the double dual

Show that $v \mapsto \mathrm{ev}_v$, with $\mathrm{ev}_v(\alpha) = \alpha(v)$, is an injective linear map $V \to
V^{**}$, hence an isomorphism when $\dim V < \infty$.
:::

::: {.callout-note .solution collapse="true" title="Solution"}
Linearity: $\mathrm{ev}_{v + \lambda w}(\alpha) = \alpha(v) + \lambda\alpha(w)$. Injectivity: if $v \neq 0$, extend
$v$ to a basis and let $\alpha$ be the dual basis element with $\alpha(v) = 1$; then $\mathrm{ev}_v \neq 0$. Since
$\dim V^{**} = \dim V^* = \dim V$ by @exr-dual-dimension, an injective linear map between spaces of the same finite
dimension is bijective (rank-nullity).
:::

::: {.callout-tip .verification collapse="true" title="Verification"}

### The dual basis

A basis of $V$ singles out a basis of $V^*$: the functionals that return the coordinates. The definition states the
Kronecker-delta property that characterises them and records that every covector expands in this basis with
coefficients given by its values on the original basis.

:::: {.statement-box}
::: {#def-dual-basis}
#### Dual basis

Given a basis $e_1, \dots, e_n$ of $V$, the **dual basis** $e^1, \dots, e^n$ of $V^*$ consists of the functionals
with $e^i(e_j) = \delta^i_j$ (equal to $1$ if $i = j$ and $0$ otherwise). Then $e^i(v) = v^i$ is the $i$-th
coordinate of $v$, and $\alpha = \alpha_i e^i$ with $\alpha_i = \alpha(e_i)$ for every covector.
:::

On a manifold the differentials $dx^i$ are dual to the coordinate vector fields $\partial_j$. The example records this
identification, which is the form in which the dual basis appears in every later chapter.

basis $dx^1, \dots, dx^n$ of coordinate differentials, $dx^i(\partial_j) = \delta^i_j$ (@sec-one-forms).
:::

Computing a dual basis by hand means inverting the matrix of the basis. The exercise does this for $f$ and uses the
result to recover the coordinates of $(5, 4)$ without solving a system.

::: {#exr-dual-basis}
#### Dual basis of a non-standard basis

Find the dual basis of $f_1 = (2, 1)$, $f_2 = (1, 2)$ and use it to read off the coordinates of $(5, 4)$.

::: {.callout-note .solution collapse="true" title="Solution"}
Write the dual basis vectors as rows $f^1, f^2$; the conditions $f^i(f_j) = \delta^i_j$ say that the matrix with
rows $f^i$ times the matrix with columns $f_j$ is the identity, so the rows are the rows of the inverse matrix.
The coordinates are $f^1(v) = 2$, $f^2(v) = 1$, as in @fig-basis-change:

{{< sage exr-dual-basis >}}
:::

Changing the basis of $V$ changes its dual basis, and the two change in opposite ways. The exercise derives the rule
and extracts from it the transformation laws of vector and covector components, which is where the words covariant and
contravariant come from.

::: {#exr-dual-basis-transform}
#### How the dual basis transforms

If $e'_j = A^i{}_j e_i$ is a new basis, show that the new dual basis is $e'^i = (A^{-1})^i{}_j e^j$: vectors'
components transform with $A^{-1}$, covectors' components with $A$.
:::

::: {.callout-note .solution collapse="true" title="Solution"}
$(A^{-1})^i{}_k e^k(e'_j) = (A^{-1})^i{}_k A^k{}_j = \delta^i_j$, so these functionals satisfy the defining
property and are the dual basis by uniqueness. For a vector $v = v^j e_j = v'^i e'_i$, applying $e'^i$ gives $v'^i
= (A^{-1})^i{}_j v^j$; for a covector, $\alpha'_j = \alpha(e'_j) = A^i{}_j \alpha_i$. The two transformation laws
are the origin of the words contravariant and covariant in @def-tensor-type.
:::

::: {.callout-tip .verification collapse="true" title="Verification"}

The kernel vector of the running matrix $A$ and the proportionality of its rows are the first facts collected in this
section. The proposition states them; together they fix the rank and the nullity of $A$.

of $A$ is twice the first.

A single kernel vector already bounds the rank, and the proportional rows pin it down. The example draws the
rank-nullity consequences: rank one, nullity two, and a kernel that is a plane.

::: {#exm-kernel-rank-nullity}
#### What the kernel vector tells about the rank

The kernel contains a non-zero vector, so the nullity is at least $1$ and the rank at most $2$; the proportional
rows show that the rank is exactly $1$, and rank-nullity gives nullity $2$: the kernel is a plane, and $(1, 1, -1)$
is one of its directions.
:::

::: {#exm-kernel-lean-route}
#### More kernel vectors

Every multiple $t(1, 1, -1)$ lies in the kernel, since $A(t v) = t A v = 0$, and so does $(-2, 1, 0)$: $1 \cdot (-2) +
2 \cdot 1 + 3 \cdot 0 = 0$ and $2 \cdot (-2) + 4 \cdot 1 + 6 \cdot 0 = 0$. The two directions $(1, 1, -1)$ and
$(-2, 1, 0)$ are not proportional, as a plane requires.
:::

`la-independence.sage`: Sage finds a non-singular minor of the family (independence) or a rational relation among the vectors (dependence); Lean evaluates the minor's determinant or the relation.

`la-span-ker.sage`: Sage checks that the family lies in the kernel and has its dimension, and reads a kernel vector's coordinates off a non-singular minor; Lean checks them from the kernel equations.
:::

The proportional rows of $A$ are the reason its rank is one, and this is a general fact about $2 \times n$ matrices.
The exercise asks for the proof, which identifies the rank with the dimension of the row space.

::: {#exr-kernel-rows-rank}
#### Proportional rows and rank one

Prove that a non-zero $2 \times n$ matrix has rank $1$ exactly when its two rows are proportional.
:::

::: {.callout-note .solution collapse="true" title="Solution"}
The rank is the dimension of the row space (equal to that of the column space). Two rows span a space of dimension
$1$ exactly when they are dependent, that is, when one is a multiple of the other, since both cannot vanish. For
$A$, the second row is $2$ times the first, so the rank is $1$.
:::

::: {.callout-tip .verification collapse="true" title="Verification"}

A second kernel vector can be checked in the same two lines as the first. The exercise asks for that check and for
the reason the two vectors together span the kernel.

::: {#exr-kernel-second-vector}
#### A second kernel vector

Show that $(3, 0, -1)$ is in the kernel of $A$ and that it is not a multiple of $(1, 1, -1)$.
:::

::: {.callout-note .solution collapse="true" title="Solution"}
The two components of $A(3, 0, -1)^{\mathsf{T}}$ are $3 + 0 - 3 = 0$ and $6 + 0 - 6 = 0$. A multiple of $(1, 1, -
1)$ has equal first two entries, which $(3, 0, -1)$ does not, so the two kernel vectors are independent and span the
two-dimensional kernel.
:::

Behind the dual basis of $f$ stands a $2 \times 2$ matrix product. The example performs it and reads the four entries
as the four values $f^i(f_j)$.

::: {#exm-dualbasis-f-product}
#### The product behind the dual basis

$\tfrac13\begin{pmatrix} 2 & -1 \\ -1 & 2 \end{pmatrix}\begin{pmatrix} 2 & 1 \\ 1 & 2 \end{pmatrix} = \tfrac13
\begin{pmatrix} 3 & 0 \\ 0 & 3 \end{pmatrix} = 1$: the diagonal entries are $f^1(f_1) = f^2(f_2) = 1$ and the
off-diagonal ones $f^1(f_2) = f^2(f_1) = 0$.
:::

#### Applying the dual basis

Use the dual basis of $f$ to find the coordinates of $(1, 5)$ and of $(-1, 1)$, and compare with
@exr-coords-f-other.

::: {.callout-note .solution collapse="true" title="Solution"}
$f^1(1, 5) = \tfrac13(2 - 5) = -1$, $f^2(1, 5) = \tfrac13(-1 + 10) = 3$; $f^1(-1, 1) = \tfrac13(-2 - 1) = -1$,
$f^2(-1, 1) = \tfrac13(1 + 2) = 1$. These agree with the solutions of the linear systems: the dual basis is the
inverse matrix applied row by row.
:::

::: {#exr-dual-f-check}
#### Checking the dual basis by hand

Verify entry by entry that the rows $f^1, f^2$ of @exm-dual-f satisfy $f^i(f_j) = \delta^i_j$.
:::

::: {.callout-note .solution collapse="true" title="Solution"}
$f^1(f_1) = \tfrac13(4 - 1) = 1$, $f^1(f_2) = \tfrac13(2 - 2) = 0$, $f^2(f_1) = \tfrac13(-2 + 2) = 0$, $f^2(f_2) =
\tfrac13(-1 + 4) = 1$. These are the four entries of the product $F^{-1} F = 1$ of @exm-dualbasis-f-product.
:::

## Bilinear forms {#sec-bilinear-forms}

A bilinear form assigns a number to two vectors, linearly in each. This section treats bilinear forms on a fixed
vector space, their symmetry, non-degeneracy and signature, with the Euclidean dot product and the Minkowski form
of special relativity as the running examples; the light cone of @fig-minkowski-cone is the picture to keep in mind.
Four definitions and one proposition on the values of the Minkowski form; a degenerate form on the plane serves as
the counterexample throughout.

### Bilinear forms

Two vectors in, one number out, linearly in each slot: this is the structure the rest of the chapter is about. The
definition fixes the component convention $B_{ij} = B(e_i, e_j)$, under which such a map is a square matrix once a
basis is chosen, and every metric tensor in the lectures follows it.

:::: {.statement-box}
::: {#def-bilinear-form}
#### Bilinear form

A **bilinear form** on $V$ is a map $B : V \times V \to \mathbb{R}$ linear in each argument separately. Its
**components** in a basis are $B_{ij} = B(e_i, e_j)$, and $B(v, w) = B_{ij} v^i w^j$: a bilinear form is an
$n \times n$ matrix once a basis is chosen.
:::

:::: {.callout-note .examples-fold collapse="true" title="Examples"}
The first instance everyone meets is the Euclidean inner product of $\mathbb{R}^n$. Its components are the Kronecker
delta, so in the standard basis its matrix is the identity.

::: {#exm-bilinear-dot}
#### The dot product

$B(v, w) = v^1 w^1 + \dots + v^n w^n$ on $\mathbb{R}^n$ is bilinear with components $\delta_{ij}$, the identity
matrix.
:::

The second instance is the one special relativity is built on, with one positive sign and three negative ones. The
example records two values, a unit timelike vector and a null one, that @prp-minkowski-values collects.

::: {#exm-bilinear-minkowski}
#### The Minkowski form

$\eta(v, w) = v^0 w^0 - v^1 w^1 - v^2 w^2 - v^3 w^3$ on $\mathbb{R}^4$ is bilinear with components
$\eta_{\mu\nu} = \mathrm{diag}(1, -1, -1, -1)$; $\eta(w, w) = 1$ for $w = (1, 0, 0, 0)$ and $\eta(v, v) = 0$ for
$v = (1, 1, 0, 0)$ (@prp-minkowski-values).
:::

Not every such form is symmetric, and the third example shows two ways to build one that is not. A product of two
covectors has rank one, and the $2 \times 2$ determinant changes sign when its arguments are swapped.

::: {#exm-bilinear-general}
#### Products of functionals and antisymmetric forms

For covectors $\alpha, \beta$, $B(v, w) = \alpha(v)\beta(w)$ is bilinear with components $\alpha_i \beta_j$; the
determinant $B(v, w) = v^1 w^2 - v^2 w^1$ on $\mathbb{R}^2$ is bilinear with $B(w, v) = -B(v, w)$. Bilinear forms
need not be symmetric.
:::

Bilinearity fails as soon as a constant is added or an absolute value appears. The exercise presents four candidate
expressions on the plane and asks which are bilinear, with a specific counterexample for each one that is not.

::: {#exr-bilinear-check}
#### Which maps are bilinear?

Decide which of the following are bilinear forms on $\mathbb{R}^2$: $v \cdot w + 1$; $v^1 w^2$; $|v|\,|w|$;
$v^1 w^1 - 3 v^2 w^1$.
:::

::: {.callout-note .solution collapse="true" title="Solution"}
$v^1 w^2$ and $v^1 w^1 - 3v^2 w^1$ are bilinear (each is a sum of products of one component of $v$ and one of
$w$). $v \cdot w + 1$ is not: $B(0, w) = 1 \neq 0$. $|v|\,|w|$ is not: $B(-v, w) = |v|\,|w| \neq -B(v, w)$.
:::

::: {.callout-tip .verification collapse="true" title="Verification"}

Reading the component matrix off an explicit formula and evaluating the form on two vectors in both orders is the
basic skill. The exercise does this for a non-symmetric form, so that $B(v, w)$ and $B(w, v)$ come out different.

::: {#exr-bilinear-matrix}
#### Components of a bilinear form

Find the components $B_{ij}$ of $B(v, w) = v^1 w^1 + 2 v^1 w^2 - v^2 w^1$ on $\mathbb{R}^2$, evaluate $B(v, w)$ and
$B(w, v)$ for $v = (1, 3)$, $w = (2, -1)$, and decide whether $B$ is symmetric.
:::

::: {.callout-note .solution collapse="true" title="Solution"}
$B_{ij}$ is the coefficient of $v^i w^j$: $B = \begin{pmatrix} 1 & 2 \\ -1 & 0 \end{pmatrix}$. Then $B(v, w) = v^{\mathsf
T} B w = -6$ while $B(w, v) = 15$, so $B$ is not symmetric:

{{< sage exr-bilinear-matrix >}}
:::

Components of a bilinear form transform with two factors of the change-of-basis matrix. The exercise derives the rule
$B' = A^{\mathsf{T}} B A$ and applies it to the dot product in the basis $f$, producing the Gram matrix that the final
exercises return to.

::: {#exr-bilinear-change-basis}
#### Components under a change of basis

Show that under $e'_j = A^i{}_j e_i$ the components become $B'_{ij} = A^k{}_i A^l{}_j B_{kl}$, that is, $B' =
A^{\mathsf{T}} B A$, and compute the components of the dot product of $\mathbb{R}^2$ in the basis $f$.
:::

::: {.callout-note .solution collapse="true" title="Solution"}
$B'_{ij} = B(e'_i, e'_j) = B(A^k{}_i e_k, A^l{}_j e_l) = A^k{}_i A^l{}_j B_{kl}$ by bilinearity. For the dot
product and $A$ the matrix with columns $f_1, f_2$, $B' = A^{\mathsf{T}} A = \begin{pmatrix} 5 & 4 \\ 4 & 5
\end{pmatrix}$, the Gram matrix of $f$; $|v|^2 = 41$ comes out the same from standard coordinates and from the
$f$-coordinates $(2, 1)$:

{{< sage exr-bilinear-change-basis >}}
:::

### Symmetric forms

Most forms in geometry are symmetric, and for them the values on single vectors already determine everything. The
definition states the symmetry condition and the polarisation identity that recovers $B(v, w)$ from the quadratic form
$B(v, v)$.

:::: {.statement-box}
::: {#def-symmetric-form}
#### Symmetric bilinear form

A bilinear form is **symmetric** if $B(v, w) = B(w, v)$, that is, $B_{ij} = B_{ji}$. A symmetric form is
determined by its values $B(v, v)$ on single vectors (its **quadratic form**), by $2B(v, w) = B(v + w, v + w) -
B(v, v) - B(w, w)$.
:::

::: {.callout-tip .verification collapse="true" title="Verification"}

A quadratic polynomial in two variables encodes a symmetric matrix, with half the mixed coefficient off the diagonal.
The example extracts the matrix $S$ from $x^2 + 4xy + 4y^2$ and shows that this form never takes a negative value.

::: {#exm-symmetric-quadratic}
#### Reading a form off its quadratic form

The quadratic form $Q(x, y) = x^2 + 4xy + 4y^2$ comes from the symmetric matrix $S = \begin{pmatrix} 1 & 2 \\ 2 & 4
\end{pmatrix}$: the off-diagonal entry is half the coefficient of $xy$. Since $Q = (x + 2y)^2$, $Q \geq 0$
everywhere, with $Q = 0$ exactly on the line $x = -2y$.
:::

`sos.sage`: Sage factors the quadratic form as the square $(x + 2y)^2$, the term of the emitted `linear_combination`.

At the opposite extreme stand the forms that change sign when their arguments are exchanged, whose quadratic form
vanishes identically. The example names the two-forms of differential geometry and the electromagnetic field strength
as the instances that later chapters rely on.

::: {#exm-symmetric-not}
#### Antisymmetric forms

The determinant form $v^1 w^2 - v^2 w^1$ is antisymmetric, not symmetric, and its quadratic form is identically
zero; antisymmetric bilinear forms are the two-forms of @sec-forms, and the field strength $F_{\mu\nu}$ of
electromagnetism is one.
:::

Extracting a symmetric matrix from a quadratic form in three variables follows the same rule as in two. The exercise
asks for the matrix and for one value of the form, which turns out negative while other values are positive.

::: {#exr-symmetric-quadratic}
#### The symmetric matrix of a quadratic form

Find the symmetric matrix of $Q(x, y, z) = 2x^2 - 3xy + y^2 + 4yz$ and the value $Q(1, 2, -1)$.
:::

::: {.callout-note .solution collapse="true" title="Solution"}
Diagonal entries are the coefficients of the squares and off-diagonal entries half the mixed coefficients:
$\begin{pmatrix} 2 & -\tfrac32 & 0 \\ -\tfrac32 & 1 & 2 \\ 0 & 2 & 0 \end{pmatrix}$. $Q(1, 2, -1) = 2 - 6 + 4 - 8 = -
8$; the form takes both signs, so it is not positive definite (its signature is found as in @exr-signature-3x3).
:::

::: {.callout-tip .verification collapse="true" title="Verification"}

Every bilinear form splits uniquely into a symmetric and an antisymmetric part. The exercise asks for the proof and
applies it to the non-symmetric form of @exr-bilinear-matrix, noting which part the quadratic form sees.

::: {#exr-symmetric-decompose}
#### Symmetric plus antisymmetric

Show that every bilinear form is uniquely the sum of a symmetric and an antisymmetric one, and decompose the form
of @exr-bilinear-matrix.
:::

::: {.callout-note .solution collapse="true" title="Solution"}
$B = \tfrac12(B + B^{\mathsf{T}}) + \tfrac12(B - B^{\mathsf{T}})$, and if $B = S + A$ with $S$ symmetric and $A$
antisymmetric then $B^{\mathsf{T}} = S - A$, which forces $S = \tfrac12(B + B^{\mathsf{T}})$. For $B =
\begin{pmatrix} 1 & 2 \\ -1 & 0 \end{pmatrix}$: $S = \begin{pmatrix} 1 & \tfrac12 \\ \tfrac12 & 0 \end{pmatrix}$ and
$A = \begin{pmatrix} 0 & \tfrac32 \\ -\tfrac32 & 0 \end{pmatrix}$. Only $S$ contributes to the quadratic form.
:::

::: {.callout-tip .verification collapse="true" title="Verification"}
**Veriphy.** Recipe `matrix_from_goal`, certificate `la-matrix.sage` (`decompose_B`, `decompose_parts`, `antisym_part_quadratic`); Test (kernel-checked, 3 instances); script `la-decomposition-unique-test.sage` (`decomposition_unique`).

**Lean.**

The identity that recovers $B(v, w)$ from the quadratic form can be tested numerically, and its proof is a two-line
expansion. The exercise checks it on random vectors for the Minkowski form and explains why it says nothing about an
antisymmetric form.

::: {#exr-polarisation}
#### The polarisation identity

Check the identity $2B(v, w) = B(v + w, v + w) - B(v, v) - B(w, w)$ for the Minkowski form on random integer
vectors, and show why it fails to recover an antisymmetric form.
:::

::: {.callout-note .solution collapse="true" title="Solution"}
Expanding by bilinearity, $B(v + w, v + w) = B(v, v) + B(v, w) + B(w, v) + B(w, w)$, and symmetry turns the two
middle terms into $2B(v, w)$. For an antisymmetric form the middle terms cancel instead, and the right-hand side
is $0$ whatever $B(v, w)$ is:

{{< sage exr-polarisation >}}
:::

### Non-degenerate forms

![The Minkowski form $\eta(v, v) = t^2 - x^2$ on $\mathbb{R}^2$: the light cone $\eta = 0$ and the timelike
($\eta > 0$) and spacelike ($\eta < 0$) regions. Generated by
`figures/minkowski_cone.sage`.](figures/minkowski_cone.svg){#fig-minkowski-cone width=45%}

{{< interactive minkowski_cone 520 >}}

A form may have directions that pair to zero with everything, and when it has none it identifies vectors with
covectors. The definition names this property, gives the determinant test, and introduces the lowering and raising of
indices; the light cone above is the picture for the Minkowski form.

:::: {.statement-box}
::: {#def-nondegenerate}
#### Non-degenerate bilinear form

A bilinear form is **non-degenerate** if $B(v, w) = 0$ for all $w$ forces $v = 0$; equivalently its matrix
$B_{ij}$ is invertible, $\det B \neq 0$. A non-degenerate form identifies $V$ with $V^*$ by $v \mapsto B(v, \cdot)$,
which in components is **lowering an index**, $v_i = B_{ij} v^j$; the inverse matrix $B^{ij}$ **raises** it.
:::

::: {.callout-tip .verification collapse="true" title="Verification"}

`la-raise-lower-test.sage` (kernel-checked instances): raising undoes lowering, B⁻¹(B v) = v, at n = 0, at the Gram matrix of f and at η (Sage supplies B⁻¹).

$V$ with $V^*$ (@exr-minkowski-signature).

With $\eta$, lowering flips the sign of the spatial components, while with $\delta_{ij}$ it changes nothing. The
example works one case and explains why the position of an index goes unnoticed in Euclidean space.

::: {#exm-nondegenerate-lowering}
#### Lowering an index

With $\eta$, the vector $v^\mu = (1, 1, 0, 0)$ has covector $v_\mu = \eta_{\mu\nu} v^\nu = (1, -1, 0, 0)$; with the
Euclidean $\delta_{ij}$, lowering does nothing, which is why index position is invisible in Euclidean space.
:::

A single four-vector is enough to practise moving an index down and back up with $\eta$. The exercise asks for the
covector, the vector recovered from it, and the invariant $v_\mu v^\mu$, whose sign classifies the vector.

::: {#exr-lower-index}
#### Lowering and raising

Lower the index of $v^\mu = (2, 1, 0, 3)$ with $\eta$, raise it again with $\eta^{\mu\nu}$, and compute
$v_\mu v^\mu$. Is $v$ timelike, spacelike or null?
:::

::: {.callout-note .solution collapse="true" title="Solution"}
$v_\mu = \eta_{\mu\nu} v^\nu = (2, -1, 0, -3)$; since $\eta^{-1} = \eta$, raising gives back $(2, 1, 0, 3)$;
$v_\mu v^\mu = 4 - 1 - 0 - 9 = -6 < 0$, so $v$ is spacelike.

:::

The determinant test applies to any symmetric matrix. The exercise runs it on three forms, including the degenerate
$S$, and asks for the kernel vectors of the degenerate one.

::: {#exr-nondegenerate-test}
#### Testing non-degeneracy

Decide which of $\mathrm{diag}(1, -1, -1, -1)$, $\begin{pmatrix} 1 & 2 \\ 2 & 4 \end{pmatrix}$ and
$\begin{pmatrix} 2 & 1 & 0 \\ 1 & 2 & 1 \\ 0 & 1 & 2 \end{pmatrix}$ are non-degenerate, and find the vectors that
pair to zero with everything for the degenerate one.
:::

::: {.callout-note .solution collapse="true" title="Solution"}
The determinants are $-1$, $0$ and $4$, so the first and third are non-degenerate. For the second, the kernel is
the line through $(1, -\tfrac12)$, equivalently $(2, -1)$, and indeed $(2, -1) \cdot S e_1 = 2 - 2 = 0$, $(2, -1)
\cdot S e_2 = 4 - 4 = 0$:

{{< sage exr-nondegenerate-test >}}
:::

The identification of $V$ with $V^*$ by a non-degenerate form is a linear isomorphism, and this exercise proves it.
Injectivity is non-degeneracy restated; rank-nullity supplies surjectivity.

::: {#exr-nondegenerate-iso}
#### Non-degeneracy as an isomorphism

Show that $v \mapsto B(v, \cdot)$ is a linear map $V \to V^*$, that it is injective exactly when $B$ is
non-degenerate, and that it is then an isomorphism for finite-dimensional $V$.
:::

::: {.callout-note .solution collapse="true" title="Solution"}
Linearity in the first argument makes $v \mapsto B(v, \cdot)$ linear, and each $B(v, \cdot)$ is a functional by
linearity in the second. Its kernel is $\{v : B(v, w) = 0 \ \forall w\}$, which is $\{0\}$ exactly by the
definition of non-degeneracy. An injective linear map between spaces of equal finite dimension ($\dim V^* = \dim
V$) is surjective by rank-nullity. In components the map is $v^j \mapsto B_{ij} v^j$, invertible when $\det B \neq
0$, with inverse $B^{ij}$.
:::

::: {.callout-tip .verification collapse="true" title="Verification"}
